etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese arayuru, the attributive form of the passive form of ar- “to be, to exist”. Note that the passive marker -(a)ye- (attributive form -(a)yuru) ceased to be used in Early Middle Japanese except in fossilized expressions such as あらゆる (arayuru) and いはゆる (ifayuru) and in kanbun.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Negative form of 行ける (ikeru), the potential form of 行く (iku).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Alteration of おおせある (ōse aru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 御(お) (o-, honorific prefix) + 洒(しゃ)落(れ) (share)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Clipping of けれども (keredomo, “although, but”).
First attested in 1711.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Unknown.
Possible analyses include:
* Related to しゃぶしゃぶ (shabushabu), itself apparently an onomatopoeia.
* Derived as intensifying prefix しゃ (sha) attaching to a root form related to べりべり (beriberi, “talkatively; a talkative person”), べらべら (berabera, “bubblingly; talkatively”), べろ (bero, “tongue”).
Listed in the Nippo Jisho of 1603. Earliest appearance may be in the early 1300s during the Kamakura period.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From そう (sō, “like that, so”) + 言(い)えば (ieba, conditional form of 言(い)う (iu, “to say”)). Literally, “speaking of that....”

etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 上 (MC dzyangX) + 京 (MC kjaeng).

etymologies.text: 中 (naka, chū, “middle”) + 指 (yubi, shi, “finger”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 別 (betsu, “separate”) + に (ni, particle), literally separately, used idiomatically to mean something closer to especially. Compare Korean 별로 (byeollo).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Sinitic 反對.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 受(う)ける (ukeru, “to receive”) + 取(と)る (toru, “to take”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 句読(くとう) (kutō) + 点(てん) (ten).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 女王 (nrjo^X hjwang, literally “female + king”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Alteration of joō.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 女王 (nrjo^X hjwang, literally “female + king”). The goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Usually considered a compound of 実(み) (mi, “fruit”) + 乗(の)る (noru, “to ride”). Alternatively, noru may be a corruption of なる (naru, “to become; to bear fruit”); compare the form 実(みな)る (minaru), attested in the Nihon Shoki.

etymologies.text: 小(こ) (ko-, “little”) + 銭(ぜに) (zeni, “coins; money”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 左(さ) (sa, “left”) + 右(ゆう) (yū, “right”).

poru > ɸoru > horu.
Doublet of 掘(ほ)る (horu, “to dig”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Coined by Japanese philosopher and politician Nishi Amane as a translation of English will, and became established by being included in the 哲学字彙 (Tetsugaku Jii, “Dictionary of Philosophy”) by Inoue Tetsujirō.

etymologies.text: Middle Chinese 標識

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Calque of German Volkslied.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Appears in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE.
Ultimate derivation possibly borrowed from Ainu サロ (saro, “monkey”, from サㇻ (sar, “a tail”) + オ (o, “to bear, to wear, to carry”)).
The kanji is from Chinese 猿 (yuán, “ape”). Compare Japanese 猪 (inoshishi, “boar”) from Chinese 猪 (zhū, “pig”) and Japanese 豚 (buta, “pig”) from Chinese 豚 (tún, “suckling pig”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Appears in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE, used phonetically to spell the sound /masi/.
Ultimate derivation unknown.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Derived from earlier mashi form above. Found in texts from the early 1900s, possibly earlier. Appears to be mashi + the pluralizing and genericizing suffix ら (ra).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 猿 (MC hjwon).
The kan'on pronunciation, so likely a later borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨ko₁⟩ → */kwo/ → /ko/
From Old Japanese. Used phonetically to spell ko in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Appears to be 粉 (ko, “powder”, see above) + な (-na, suffixing element, meaning unclear).
First cited to 1683.

etymologies.text: 羊(よう) (yō, “sheep”) + 毛(もう) (mō, “hair”)

etymologies.text: Compare Proto-Ryukyuan *oe-pito, using native elements.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: By surface analysis, 職(しょく) (shoku) + 業(ぎょう) (-gyō).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kupu/ → */kuwu/ → /kuu/
From Old Japanese. from Proto-Japonic *kup-.
The medial /w/ vanishes because Japanese does not have a /wu/ phoneme. It surfaces though in various conjugations, such as the negative form kuwanai or the passive form kuwareru.
Possibly cognate with 口(くち) (kuchi, “mouth”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 高(たか) (taka, root of 高(たか)い (takai, “high, tall”)) + まる (-maru, “to become (an adjective), -en”), developed from Classical Japanese 高む.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally a compound of 根 (ne, “root”, more specifically signifying somewhere hidden away) + 住み (sumi, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 住む sumu, “to live in a place, to reside”), meaning roughly “one who lives in hidden places”. The sumi changes to zumi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Abbreviation of nezumi. Used in some compounds.
